title: Liquid Phase Electron Microscopy Study of the Atomic Dynamics of Electrified Solid-liquid Interfaces
content: Liquid phase electron microscopy (LPEM) allowing in situ imaging of the morphology, structure, formation and transformation dynamics of materials in liquid environments by overcoming the limitations of conventional electron microscopy imaging in high-vacuum environments has attracted broad interest from materials science to chemistry, biology, and other fields. The advanced liquid cell development has been a key enabler for the expanded LPEM capabilities of high-resolution imaging and revealing the fundamental mechanisms of complex reactions. We recently developed polymer electrochemical liquid cells for in situ TEM study of electrocatalysts’ structural evolution during reactions and the behavior of electrified solid-liquid interfaces. By implementing the thin polymer membranes in the electrochemical liquid cells, it enables the in situ atomic resolution imaging of Cu catalysts’ surface restructuring during CO2 electroreduction reactions (CO2RR) [1]. It also allows detailed chemical analysis using electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) by rapidly freezing the samples without breaking the membranes. This approach establishes an in situ electrochemical (EC)-TEM platform [2] for innovative studies of electrochemical reactions and electrocatalysis through correlated in situ LPEM atomic imaging and cryogenic-EM spectroscopic analysis (Fig. 1).
